results.corrected_extracted: Smoking and breathing, single studies as the review relays them: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (Kempker 2015; US adults; retrospective data analysis): cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days in 16.9%, 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of people who smoked cannabis on 0, 1–5, 6–20 and more than 20 of the past 30 days, and wheeze in the past year in 12.4%, 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (as printed, unadjusted); more than 20 joint-years against no exposure, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (95% CI 1.1 to 3.9), with no association at lower cumulative exposure. Vancouver (Tan 2009; random sample of 878 people aged 40 or more, spirometry): people who had smoked at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco were not at significantly greater risk of COPD or respiratory symptoms; people who had smoked both had higher odds of COPD (OR 2.90, 1.53 to 5.51) and of symptoms (OR 2.39, 1.58 to 3.62), adjusted for age, asthma and comorbidities; the review does not name the comparison group, and its text calls this smoking cannabis in a joint combined with tobacco while its Table 4 describes people who smoked both. South Island of New Zealand (Hancox 2010; 1,037 people followed to age 32): cumulative use associated with higher FVC, lung volumes and airway resistance but not with FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio or gas transfer. Tashkin 2012 (299 people followed 9.8 years; the review gives no place): more chronic bronchitis at follow-up with continued cannabis smoking than in never or former smokers. Naples (Fiorelli 2013; people treated for spontaneous pneumothorax, 13 who smoked cannabis and 140 who did not, 135 of them tobacco smokers): bullae in 8 (62%) against 110 (78%) overall and, under age 35, in 7 of 10 against 3 of 10, though the text says cannabis smoking predisposed to bullous lung disease.
results.note: All numbers match Table 4 (rendered pp. 1342-1346) and the text. Wording only: the review labels Kempker a retrospective data analysis (not one of its cross-sectional surveys) and names neither Dunedin nor Los Angeles.

results.corrected_extracted: Routes compared in laboratory studies (second-hand): Newmeyer 2017 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally; smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis in separate sessions): smoking produced significantly greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h after dosing; route had no significant effect on breathing rate or blood pressure; heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, increases that did not differ significantly between routes. Cooper and Haney 2009 (24 healthy volunteers; blunts against joints of the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent. The review's Discussion gives the Newmeyer sample as n = 11, against 11 and 9 in its Table 4.
results.note: Numbers match Table 4 (rendered pp. 1342, 1344), the text and the Discussion. The review states a within-subject design only for Newmeyer, none for Cooper and Haney, so 'in the same people' says more than the review.

results.corrected_extracted: Vaping in the review (second-hand): three empirical studies have a vaping arm, and all compare vaping with smoking (Newmeyer 2017 also with placebo). Newmeyer 2017 (the laboratory crossover; dried cannabis in a vaporizer). Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post design, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness during the trial had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007 as printed), while FEV1 did not change significantly (p = 0.053 as printed); the amount used a day fell slightly and not significantly (p = 0.10 as printed), though the text says vaping reduced it. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape for longer than a month, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

results.corrected_extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled and no appraisal is reported (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

Lifetime frequency, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). results.corrected_extracted: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on cannabis or tobacco use before conscription and none after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the heavy group reported some tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting of cannabis use, while anecdotal information suggests some men inflated their use to be exempted from military training. Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) gave unstable or inestimable results, because most people who used cannabis, especially frequently, also used tobacco and lung cancer was uncommon. The authors argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null. Their conclusion calls the finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise lung cancer risk, and the Discussion proposes its use in drug-prevention programmes. Editors' note: later tobacco smoking, if more common in the men who used cannabis, would bias the estimate away from the null; the paper names later changes in tobacco use only in its toward-the-null argument, whose examples concern cannabis alone.
results.corrected_locator: Results, last paragraph (Supplemental Tables 1–2; pp. 6-7); Discussion, 4th paragraph (drug prevention programmes; p. 7) and 6th paragraph (limitations; p. 8); Conclusions
results.note: Author statements match. But the paper does say post-conscription changes in 'marijuana or tobacco use' push toward the null, so 'covers this only as residual confounding' is inexact. Discussion 3rd and 5th paragraphs hold none of this content.

results.corrected_extracted: Oral route in the review (second-hand): five empirical studies have an oral arm. In adults, the Newmeyer 2017 laboratory crossover found heart rate 13.0 and 10.2 beats a minute above placebo at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different from smoked or vaporised cannabis, and no effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; in the Shiplo 2016 survey of 364 Canadian medical cannabis patients, eating was rated lower in perceived respiratory harm than smoking. The other three are records of exposures, two of them in children only: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, 2013 to 2015): tachycardia in 84 (printed as 31%, which 430 cannot give), hypertension, chest pain or hypotension in a few, and respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger; Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support; Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common, with severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at recorded doses above 2 mg/kg of body weight. The Abstract nonetheless says cannabis edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects, and the Discussion that severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes. No included study measured lung function or breathing symptoms in adults who eat cannabis against adults who do not use it.
results.note: Numbers match rendered Table 4 and text. The review gives no age mix for Cao's 430 exposures (all ages, analysed by age), so 'mostly in young children' says more than it; its hypertension entry is restored. 84/430 = 19.5%.
